claim: Pancreatic adenosquamous carcinoma (PASC) constitutes 1–4% of pancreatic exocrine tumors.
source: Pancreatic adenosquamous carcinoma (PASC) is a rare and aggressive disease that constitutes 1–4% of pancreatic exocrine tumors (Madura et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Madura et al., 1999

claim: PASC patient median survival is 8 months.
source: Patient prognosis is extremely poor, with a median survival of 8 months (Simone et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Simone et al., 2013

claim: Liu et al., 2014 reported high-frequency mutations affecting UPF1 in 78% (18 of 23) of PASC patients.
source: Liu et al., 2014 reported high-frequency mutations affecting UPF1, which encodes a core component of the nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway, in 78% (18 of 23) of PASC patients.
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2014 and specific numerical data

claim: UPF1 mutations reported by Liu et al. were absent from patient-matched normal pancreatic tissue (0 of 18).
source: These mutations were absent from patient-matched normal pancreatic tissue (0 of 18) and from non-PASC tumors (0 of 29 non-adenosquamous pancreatic carcinomas and 0 of 21 lung squamous cell carcinomas).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2014 with specific numerical data

claim: UPF1 mutations reported by Liu et al. were absent from non-PASC tumors (0 of 29 non-adenosquamous pancreatic carcinomas and 0 of 21 lung squamous cell carcinomas).
source: These mutations were absent from patient-matched normal pancreatic tissue (0 of 18) and from non-PASC tumors (0 of 29 non-adenosquamous pancreatic carcinomas and 0 of 21 lung squamous cell carcinomas).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2014 with specific numerical data

claim: Three subsequent studies of distinct PASC cohorts did not report somatic mutations in UPF1.
source: Three subsequent studies of distinct PASC cohorts, however, did not report somatic mutations in UPF1 (Fang et al., 2017; Hayashi et al., 2020; Witkiewicz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to three independent studies

claim: The absence of UPF1 mutations in three subsequent studies (0 of 34 total PASC samples) is significantly different from the high rate reported by Liu et al. (18 of 23 PASC samples) with p<10−8.
source: This absence of UPF1 mutations is significantly different from the high rate reported by Liu et al. (0 of 34 total PASC samples from three cohorts [Fang et al., 2017; Hayashi et al., 2020; Witkiewicz et al., 2015] vs. 18 of 23 PASC samples from Liu et al; p<10−8 by the two-sided binomial proportion test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data from multiple cited studies

claim: The majority of UPF1 mutations reported by Liu et al. caused skipping of UPF1 exons 10 and 11.
source: Liu et al. reported that the majority of UPF1 mutations caused skipping of UPF1 exons 10 and 11, disrupting UPF1's RNA helicase domain that is essential for its NMD activity (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al. and Lee et al., 2015

claim: UPF1's RNA helicase domain is essential for its NMD activity.
source: Liu et al. reported that the majority of UPF1 mutations caused skipping of UPF1 exons 10 and 11, disrupting UPF1's RNA helicase domain that is essential for its NMD activity (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2015

claim: KPC cells are defined by mutations affecting KRAS and p53 that also occur in the vast majority of PASC cases.
source: KPC cells are defined by mutations affecting KRAS and p53 (encoded by Kras and Trp53 in mouse) that also occur in the vast majority of PASC cases (Borazanci et al., 2015; Fang et al., 2017; Hayashi et al., 2020), making them a genetically appropriate system.
evidence: Supported by citations to three studies

claim: Guide delivery resulted in the production of UPF1 mRNA lacking exons 10 and 11 in KPC cells.
source: We delivered Upf1-targeting paired guide RNAs to KPC cells using recombinant adenoviral vectors and confirmed that guide delivery resulted in the production of UPF1 mRNA lacking exons 10 and 11 and a corresponding reduction in full-length UPF1 protein levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–G

claim: Guide delivery resulted in a corresponding reduction in full-length UPF1 protein levels in KPC cells.
source: We delivered Upf1-targeting paired guide RNAs to KPC cells using recombinant adenoviral vectors and confirmed that guide delivery resulted in the production of UPF1 mRNA lacking exons 10 and 11 and a corresponding reduction in full-length UPF1 protein levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–G

claim: No significant differences in tumor volume were detected in mice implanted with control or Upf1-targeted KPC cells.
source: We detected no significant differences in tumor volume or survival in mice implanted with control or Upf1-targeted KPC cells (Figure 1B–D and Figure 1—source datas 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B–D

claim: No significant differences in survival were detected in mice implanted with control or Upf1-targeted KPC cells.
source: We detected no significant differences in tumor volume or survival in mice implanted with control or Upf1-targeted KPC cells (Figure 1B–D and Figure 1—source datas 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B–D

claim: Tumors derived from control and Upf1-targeted cells displayed similar histopathological features characteristic of moderately to poorly differentiated pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas.
source: Tumors derived from control as well as Upf1-targeted cells displayed similar histopathological features characteristic of moderately to poorly differentiated pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: Supported by histopathological analysis shown in Figure 1E–G

claim: No squamous differentiation was identified by histomorphologic evaluation in tumors from control or Upf1-targeted KPC cells.
source: No squamous differentiation was identified by histomorphologic evaluation and no expression of the squamous marker p40 (ΔNp63) was detected (Figure 1H and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by histomorphologic evaluation and IHC data shown in Figure 1H

claim: No expression of the squamous marker p40 (ΔNp63) was detected in tumors from control or Upf1-targeted KPC cells.
source: No squamous differentiation was identified by histomorphologic evaluation and no expression of the squamous marker p40 (ΔNp63) was detected (Figure 1H and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1H

claim: Inducing the reported Upf1 exon skipping in vivo had no detectable effects on pancreatic cancer growth in the KPC model.
source: We concluded that inducing the reported Upf1 exon skipping in vivo had no detectable effects on pancreatic cancer growth or acquisition of adenosquamous features in the KPC model.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in Figure 1

claim: Inducing the reported Upf1 exon skipping in vivo had no detectable effects on acquisition of adenosquamous features in the KPC model.
source: We concluded that inducing the reported Upf1 exon skipping in vivo had no detectable effects on pancreatic cancer growth or acquisition of adenosquamous features in the KPC model.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in Figure 1

claim: Minigenes are frequently spliced less efficiently than endogenous genes.
source: Minigenes are common tools for studying splicing, but they are frequently spliced less efficiently than endogenous genes, presumably because they are gene fragments that lack potentially important sequence features that promote splicing and incompletely capture the close relationship between chromatin and splicing (Luco et al., 2011; Naftelberg et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Luco et al., 2011 and Naftelberg et al., 2015

claim: IVS10+31G>A (patient 1; P1) was reportedly recurrent across three different patients.
source: We selected IVS10+31G>A (patient 1; P1) because it was reportedly recurrent across three different patients (making it equally or more common than any other mutation) and induced strong mis-splicing on its own (36% mis-spliced mRNA, versus 0% for wild-type UPF1)
evidence: Supported by reference to Liu et al.'s reported data

claim: IVS10+31G>A induced strong mis-splicing on its own (36% mis-spliced mRNA, versus 0% for wild-type UPF1) according to Liu et al.
source: We selected IVS10+31G>A (patient 1; P1) because it was reportedly recurrent across three different patients (making it equally or more common than any other mutation) and induced strong mis-splicing on its own (36% mis-spliced mRNA, versus 0% for wild-type UPF1)
evidence: Supported by reference to Liu et al.'s reported data

claim: IVS10-17G>A (patient 9; P9) had one of the strongest effects on splicing (90% mis-spliced mRNA) according to Liu et al.
source: we selected IVS10-17G>A (patient 9; P9) because it had one of the strongest effects on splicing (90% mis-spliced mRNA).
evidence: Supported by reference to Liu et al.'s reported data

claim: IVS10+31G>A was present in a homozygous state in two of the three patients carrying it according to Liu et al.
source: IVS10+31G>A was present in a homozygous state in two of the three patients carrying it, while IVS10-17G>A was present in a heterozygous state.
evidence: Supported by reference to Liu et al.'s reported data

claim: IVS10-17G>A was present in a heterozygous state according to Liu et al.
source: IVS10+31G>A was present in a homozygous state in two of the three patients carrying it, while IVS10-17G>A was present in a heterozygous state.
evidence: Supported by reference to Liu et al.'s reported data

claim: UPF1-mutant cells did not exhibit decreased NMD efficiency compared to wild-type cells.
source: We did not observe decreased NMD efficiency in UPF1-mutant versus wild-type cells; instead, UPF1-mutant cells exhibited evidence of modestly more efficient NMD, although these differences were not statistically significant (Figure 2A and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by beta-globin reporter assay data shown in Figure 2A

claim: UPF1-mutant cells exhibited evidence of modestly more efficient NMD, although these differences were not statistically significant.
source: We did not observe decreased NMD efficiency in UPF1-mutant versus wild-type cells; instead, UPF1-mutant cells exhibited evidence of modestly more efficient NMD, although these differences were not statistically significant (Figure 2A and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by beta-globin reporter assay data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Neither UPF1-mutant cell line exhibited global increases in the expression of NMD substrates relative to wild-type cells.
source: These analyses revealed that neither UPF1-mutant cell line exhibited global increases in the expression of NMD substrates relative to wild-type cells.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis of endogenous NMD substrates

claim: Both UPF1-mutant cell lines exhibited modestly lower global levels of endogenous NMD substrates than did wild-type cells.
source: Instead, both UPF1-mutant cell lines exhibited modestly lower global levels of endogenous NMD substrates than did wild-type cells, mimicking the trend observed with our NMD reporter experiments.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis of endogenous NMD substrates

claim: The tested mutations in UPF1 intron 10 do not affect NMD activity.
source: Together, these data confirm that the tested mutations in UPF1 intron 10 do not affect NMD activity (Figure 2B–D and Supplementary file 1b and c).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from NMD reporter and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B–D

claim: UPF1 mutations did not cause loss of full-length UPF1 protein.
source: Consistent with similar NMD activity independent of UPF1 mutational status, UPF1 mutations did not cause loss of full-length UPF1 protein (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2E

claim: No evidence of mis-spliced UPF1 mRNA was found in UPF1-mutant cells, except in positive control samples with spiked-in synthesized DNA.
source: We readily detected normally spliced UPF1 mRNA in all samples by RT-PCR, but found no evidence of mis-spliced UPF1 mRNA, except in positive control samples in which we spiked in synthesized DNA corresponding to the exon skipping isoform reported in Liu et al. (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, and Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2F

claim: RNA-seq analyses revealed no evidence of splice junctions consistent with the reported exon 10 and 11 skipping or other abnormal exon skipping isoforms.
source: We confirmed these results with our RNA-seq data by mapping all reads against all possible splice junctions connecting exons 9, 10, 11, and 12. These analyses revealed no evidence of splice junctions consistent with the reported exon 10 and 11 skipping or other abnormal exon skipping isoforms (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2G

claim: 45% (18 of 40) of the reported UPF1 mutations are identical to standing genetic variants in the human population.
source: We found genetic variants identical to 45% (18 of 40) of the reported UPF1 mutations, one of which is present in the reference human genome.
evidence: Supported by comparison with genetic variant databases

claim: One of the reported UPF1 mutations is present in the reference human genome.
source: We found genetic variants identical to 45% (18 of 40) of the reported UPF1 mutations, one of which is present in the reference human genome.
evidence: Supported by comparison with reference genome

claim: 89% (16 of 18) of UPF1-mutant patients had one or more reported mutations that corresponded to standing genetic variation.
source: Eighty-nine percent (16 of 18) of UPF1-mutant patients had one or more reported mutations that corresponded to standing genetic variation (Figure 3A–F and Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Supported by comparison with genetic variant databases shown in Figure 3A–F

claim: A large fraction of reported intronic UPF1 mutations were identical to standing genetic variation.
source: The distribution of overlaps between reported UPF1 mutations and standing genetic variation depended strongly upon genic context. A large fraction of reported intronic UPF1 mutations were identical to standing genetic variation, while the majority of reported exonic UPF1 mutations were not (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Supported by analysis of genetic variant databases

claim: The majority of reported exonic UPF1 mutations were not identical to standing genetic variation.
source: The distribution of overlaps between reported UPF1 mutations and standing genetic variation depended strongly upon genic context. A large fraction of reported intronic UPF1 mutations were identical to standing genetic variation, while the majority of reported exonic UPF1 mutations were not (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Supported by analysis of genetic variant databases

claim: UPF1 is essential for embryonic viability and development in mammals.
source: Second, UPF1 is essential for embryonic viability and development in mammals (Medghalchi et al., 2001), zebrafish (Wittkopp et al., 2009), and Drosophila (Avery et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Medghalchi et al., 2001

claim: UPF1 is essential for embryonic viability and development in zebrafish.
source: Second, UPF1 is essential for embryonic viability and development in mammals (Medghalchi et al., 2001), zebrafish (Wittkopp et al., 2009), and Drosophila (Avery et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wittkopp et al., 2009

claim: UPF1 is essential for embryonic viability and development in Drosophila.
source: Second, UPF1 is essential for embryonic viability and development in mammals (Medghalchi et al., 2001), zebrafish (Wittkopp et al., 2009), and Drosophila (Avery et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Avery et al., 2011

claim: Liu et al. reported that all UPF1 mutations caused mis-splicing that is expected to disable UPF1 protein function.
source: As Liu et al. reported that all UPF1 mutations caused mis-splicing that is expected to disable UPF1 protein function (Liu et al., 2014), then those mutations should be incompatible with life when present as inherited genetic variants.
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2014

claim: Two reported UPF1 mutations had no effect on UPF1 splicing when introduced into their endogenous genomic contexts.
source: Our finding that two reported mutations had no effect on UPF1 splicing when introduced into their endogenous genomic contexts offers a way to explain this incongruity, at least for the two reported lesions that we studied.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in Figure 2

claim: Primary sequencing data from patient-matched tumor and normal samples from Liu et al. were not available.
source: We contacted the senior author (Dr. YanJun Lu) to request primary sequencing data from patient-matched tumor and normal samples, but neither primary sequencing data from matched samples nor the samples themselves were available.
evidence: Based on direct communication with the senior author

claim: Somatic UPF1 mutations were identified in samples from 6 of 17 PASC patients in the Fang et al. dataset using relaxed mutation-calling criteria.
source: Using relaxed mutation-calling criteria to maximize sensitivity (details in Materials and methods), we identified somatic UPF1 mutations in samples from 6 of 17 PASC patients.
evidence: Supported by reanalysis of sequencing data from Fang et al., 2017

claim: None of the UPF1 mutations identified in the Fang et al. dataset matched the UPF1 mutations reported by Liu et al.
source: None of those UPF1 mutations matched the UPF1 mutations reported by Liu et al., and only one was present at an allelic frequency equal to the allelic frequency of mutant KRAS, which is a known driver and which we detected in samples from all PASC patients (median allelic frequencies of 12% versus 34% for UPF1 versus KRAS mutations).
evidence: Supported by reanalysis of sequencing data from Fang et al., 2017

claim: Only one UPF1 mutation in the Fang et al. dataset was present at an allelic frequency equal to the allelic frequency of mutant KRAS.
source: None of those UPF1 mutations matched the UPF1 mutations reported by Liu et al., and only one was present at an allelic frequency equal to the allelic frequency of mutant KRAS, which is a known driver and which we detected in samples from all PASC patients (median allelic frequencies of 12% versus 34% for UPF1 versus KRAS mutations).
evidence: Supported by reanalysis of sequencing data from Fang et al., 2017

claim: Median allelic frequencies were 12% for UPF1 mutations versus 34% for KRAS mutations in the Fang et al. dataset.
source: None of those UPF1 mutations matched the UPF1 mutations reported by Liu et al., and only one was present at an allelic frequency equal to the allelic frequency of mutant KRAS, which is a known driver and which we detected in samples from all PASC patients (median allelic frequencies of 12% versus 34% for UPF1 versus KRAS mutations).
evidence: Supported by reanalysis of sequencing data from Fang et al., 2017

claim: UPF1 mutations were identified in samples from 3 of 34 pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas in the Fang et al. dataset.
source: Furthermore, we also identified UPF1 mutations in samples from patients with non-adenosquamous tumors (3 of 34 pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas), whereas Liu et al. reported finding no UPF1 mutations in non-adenosquamous pancreatic cancers (0 of 29).
evidence: Supported by reanalysis of sequencing data from Fang et al., 2017

claim: UPF1 is not a frequent or adenosquamous-specific mutational target in most PASC cohorts.
source: In concert with the reports of Witkiewicz et al., 2015 and Hayashi et al., 2020 of finding no UPF1 mutations in their PASC samples, these analyses suggest that UPF1 is not a frequent or adenosquamous-specific mutational target in most PASC cohorts.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple studies and reanalysis of Fang et al. data

claim: Many reported UPF1 mutations occur as germline genetic variants of no known pathogenicity.
source: UPF1's status as an essential gene and our discovery that many reported UPF1 mutations occur as germline genetic variants of no known pathogenicity together suggest that other UPF1 mutations reported by Liu et al. could similarly represent genetic differences that do not functionally contribute to PASC.
evidence: Supported by comparison with genetic variant databases

claim: Other UPF1 mutations reported by Liu et al. could represent genetic differences that do not functionally contribute to PASC.
source: UPF1's status as an essential gene and our discovery that many reported UPF1 mutations occur as germline genetic variants of no known pathogenicity together suggest that other UPF1 mutations reported by Liu et al. could similarly represent genetic differences that do not functionally contribute to PASC.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on experimental findings and genetic variant analysis

claim: UPF1 encodes a core component of the nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway.
source: Liu et al., 2014 reported high-frequency mutations affecting UPF1, which encodes a core component of the nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway, in 78% (18 of 23) of PASC patients.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about UPF1 function

claim: Liu et al. used a combination of molecular and histological assays to find that the UPF1 mutations caused UPF1 mis-splicing, loss of UPF1 protein, and impaired NMD.
source: The authors used a combination of molecular and histological assays to find that the UPF1 mutations caused UPF1 mis-splicing, loss of UPF1 protein, and impaired NMD, resulting in stable expression of aberrant mRNAs containing premature termination codons that would normally be degraded by NMD.
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2014

claim: Liu et al. found that UPF1 mutations resulted in stable expression of aberrant mRNAs containing premature termination codons that would normally be degraded by NMD.
source: The authors used a combination of molecular and histological assays to find that the UPF1 mutations caused UPF1 mis-splicing, loss of UPF1 protein, and impaired NMD, resulting in stable expression of aberrant mRNAs containing premature termination codons that would normally be degraded by NMD.
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2014

claim: The relevant UPF1 introns are very short and well covered by whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing technologies.
source: Although these other studies relied on whole-exome and/or genome sequencing instead of targeted UPF1 gene sequencing, those technologies yield good coverage of the relevant UPF1 gene regions because the affected introns are very short.
evidence: Based on knowledge of sequencing technologies and gene structure

claim: KPC cells were obtained from Dr. Robert Vonderheide.
source: Mouse KPC cells (KrasG12D; Trp53R172H/null; Pdx1-Cre) were obtained from Dr. Robert Vonderheide and were cultured in DMEM (GIBCO) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin (GIBCO).
evidence: Direct statement about source of materials

claim: NMD substrates arising from alternative splicing are abundant and sensitive biomarkers of NMD efficiency that are internally controlled for gene expression variation.
source: We focused on NMD substrates arising from alternative splicing, as these are abundant and sensitive biomarkers of NMD efficiency that are internally controlled for gene expression variation (Feng et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Feng et al., 2015

claim: Liu et al. measured the effects of each mutation on UPF1 splicing using a minigene assay.
source: Liu et al. measured the effects of each mutation on UPF1 splicing using a minigene assay, in which each mutation was introduced into a plasmid containing a small fragment of the UPF1 gene that was subsequently transfected into 293 T cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2014

claim: Liu et al. concluded that all reported UPF1 mutations caused dramatic UPF1 mis-splicing that disrupted key protein domains that are essential for UPF1 function in NMD.
source: Liu et al. concluded that all reported UPF1 mutations caused dramatic UPF1 mis-splicing that disrupted key protein domains that are essential for UPF1 function in NMD.
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2014

claim: Minigenes are gene fragments that lack potentially important sequence features that promote splicing.
source: Minigenes are common tools for studying splicing, but they are frequently spliced less efficiently than endogenous genes, presumably because they are gene fragments that lack potentially important sequence features that promote splicing and incompletely capture the close relationship between chromatin and splicing (Luco et al., 2011; Naftelberg et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Luco et al., 2011 and Naftelberg et al., 2015

claim: Minigenes incompletely capture the close relationship between chromatin and splicing.
source: Minigenes are common tools for studying splicing, but they are frequently spliced less efficiently than endogenous genes, presumably because they are gene fragments that lack potentially important sequence features that promote splicing and incompletely capture the close relationship between chromatin and splicing (Luco et al., 2011; Naftelberg et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Luco et al., 2011 and Naftelberg et al., 2015

claim: The GenBank accession codes reported in Liu et al. corresponded to short nucleotide sequences containing UPF1 mutations, without corresponding data for patient-matched controls.
source: The GenBank accession codes reported in Liu et al. corresponded to short nucleotide sequences containing UPF1 mutations, without corresponding data for patient-matched controls.
evidence: Based on examination of GenBank records

claim: The samples from Liu et al. were not available.
source: We contacted the senior author (Dr. YanJun Lu) to request primary sequencing data from patient-matched tumor and normal samples, but neither primary sequencing data from matched samples nor the samples themselves were available.
evidence: Based on direct communication with the senior author

claim: The relevant UPF1 introns were well covered by both the whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing used by Fang et al.
source: We focused on the two loci that contained all mutations reported by Liu et al. (UPF1 exons 10-11 and exons 21–23). Because the relevant introns are very short, they were well covered by both the whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing used by Fang et al.
evidence: Based on knowledge of sequencing technologies and gene structure

claim: KRAS is a known driver mutation in PASC.
source: None of those UPF1 mutations matched the UPF1 mutations reported by Liu et al., and only one was present at an allelic frequency equal to the allelic frequency of mutant KRAS, which is a known driver and which we detected in samples from all PASC patients (median allelic frequencies of 12% versus 34% for UPF1 versus KRAS mutations).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about KRAS in pancreatic cancer

claim: Mutant KRAS was detected in samples from all PASC patients in the Fang et al. dataset.
source: None of those UPF1 mutations matched the UPF1 mutations reported by Liu et al., and only one was present at an allelic frequency equal to the allelic frequency of mutant KRAS, which is a known driver and which we detected in samples from all PASC patients (median allelic frequencies of 12% versus 34% for UPF1 versus KRAS mutations).
evidence: Supported by reanalysis of sequencing data from Fang et al., 2017

claim: Witkiewicz et al., 2015 found no UPF1 mutations in their PASC samples.
source: In concert with the reports of Witkiewicz et al., 2015 and Hayashi et al., 2020 of finding no UPF1 mutations in their PASC samples, these analyses suggest that UPF1 is not a frequent or adenosquamous-specific mutational target in most PASC cohorts.
evidence: Supported by citation to Witkiewicz et al., 2015

claim: Hayashi et al., 2020 found no UPF1 mutations in their PASC samples.
source: In concert with the reports of Witkiewicz et al., 2015 and Hayashi et al., 2020 of finding no UPF1 mutations in their PASC samples, these analyses suggest that UPF1 is not a frequent or adenosquamous-specific mutational target in most PASC cohorts.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hayashi et al., 2020
